parts.required: Using the balance sheet, identify which asset line items you would classify as earning assets and briefly justify each choice. Then calculate the bank's total earning assets for 2022 to 2025.
parts.memo:
An earning asset is an asset that generates cash simply by being held (interest, coupons, dividends, rentals), not one that only appreciates in value. [1]

Included: cash and balances with central banks (only the excess reserves above the mandatory SARB balance earn interest; vault cash and the mandatory balance earn nothing, but the template includes the whole line because the split is not disclosed); government bonds (coupons); precious metals (nil here, so no effect); derivative financial assets; other financial investments (mostly traded securities that pay dividends or coupons); loans and advances to customers (the core earning asset); investment properties (rental income). [2]

Excluded: investments in associates and joint ventures (their results are shown below operating profit, not in operating income); property and equipment (branches support operations but produce no cash); deferred income tax assets; other assets (small items that do not earn). [1]

Earning assets = cash + government bonds + precious metals + derivative assets + other financial investments + loans and advances + investment properties:
Earning assets (Rm)  |  2022  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025
Total earning assets  |  1,193,531  |  1,243,657  |  1,344,283  |  1,477,724
e.g. 2025: 64,829 + 258,831 + 0 + 21,654 + 101,544 + 1,030,577 + 289 = 1,477,724. [1]

parts.required: Calculate the bank's net interest margin (NIM) for 2022 to 2025. Discuss the trend and explain what is driving it.
parts.memo:
NIM = net interest income / earning assets. [1]

  |  2022  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025
NII (Rm)  |  36,277  |  41,470  |  41,806  |  42,878
Earning assets (Rm)  |  1,193,531  |  1,243,657  |  1,344,283  |  1,477,724
NIM  |  3.04%  |  3.33%  |  3.11%  |  2.90%

NIM rose from 3.04% to a peak of 3.33% in 2023 and has since fallen to 2.90% in 2025 (higher is better, so this is a worsening). [1]

The driver is that earning assets are growing faster than the income they generate: in 2025 NII grew only 2.6% (from 41,806 to 42,878) while earning assets grew 9.9% (from 1,344,283 to 1,477,724); interest income actually fell in 2025 while interest expense also fell only slightly. [1]

This points to an efficiency problem: the bank is not earning enough revenue from the assets it is adding (allocation of funds, falling rates compressing asset yields, or growth in low-yield assets such as government bonds). [1]

parts.required: Calculate ROA and break it down into profit margin and asset utilisation. Then calculate leverage and ROE for 2022 to 2025 (ROE = ROA x leverage). Interpret the trend and identify what is driving the change in ROE.
parts.memo:
ROA = net income / total assets = profit margin (net income / operating income) x asset utilisation (operating income / total assets); leverage = total assets / total equity; ROE = ROA x leverage = net income / total equity. [2]

  |  2022  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025
Profit margin  |  22.52%  |  22.63%  |  23.64%  |  23.28%
Asset utilisation  |  4.98%  |  5.28%  |  5.06%  |  4.74%
ROA  |  1.12%  |  1.19%  |  1.20%  |  1.10%
Leverage (x)  |  10.81  |  11.00  |  11.25  |  12.28
ROE  |  12.13%  |  13.13%  |  13.45%  |  13.55%
e.g. 2025: profit margin 17,209 / 73,924 = 23.28%; asset utilisation 73,924 / 1,558,628 = 4.74%; ROA = 1.10%; leverage 1,558,628 / 126,967 = 12.28; ROE = 1.10% x 12.28 = 13.55%. [2]

Interpretation: ROA rose from 1.12% to about 1.20% in 2023-24 but fell in 2025 to 1.10%. Profit margins are high and stable (about 23% to 24%), so profitability of operations is not the problem. Asset utilisation fell from 5.28% in 2023 to 4.74% in 2025: the assets are not generating the revenue they should, the same issue seen in the NIM. [2]

ROE has kept edging up (12.13% to 13.55%) only because leverage has risen from 10.81 to 12.28; leverage is a prudential/regulatory decision rather than operating performance, so ROE is flattered while the underlying asset productivity deteriorates (and higher leverage means more risk). Note that small changes in small numbers (e.g. asset utilisation) are large changes on a relative basis. [1]

parts.required: Calculate the bank's cost of equity using the CAPM with the data provided (use the template's beta of 0.82). Compare it with the bank's 2025 ROE and explain what this says about value creation.
parts.memo:
CAPM: cost of equity = Rf + beta x market risk premium = 8.0% + 0.82 x 7.6% = 8.0% + 6.232% = 14.23%. [2]

Common mistake: the 7.6% is already the market risk premium (market return minus risk-free rate), so it must not have the risk-free rate subtracted again (double counting). [1]

A bank creates value only if ROE above cost of equity. 2025 ROE of 13.55% is below the cost of equity of 14.23%, so the bank is (slightly) destroying value: it is not earning the return its shareholders require. ROE exceeded the cost of equity in none of the four years (the closest was 13.55% in 2025). A bank destroying value would normally trade below book (P/B below 1); the Bloomberg P/B of 1.1 does not fit this, so the cost-of-equity inputs (beta, market risk premium) or the market's expectation of improvement should be questioned. [1]

parts.required: Calculate the cost-to-income ratio, the loan-to-deposit ratio and the credit loss ratio for 2022 to 2025. Discuss each against its usual benchmark and comment on what it shows about the bank's efficiency and risk.
parts.memo:
Cost-to-income = operating expenses / operating income (benchmark about 50%; lower is better). Loan-to-deposit = loans / deposits (normal range 80% to 90%). Credit loss ratio = credit impairments / loans (normal range 1% to 3%, lower is better). [1.5]

  |  2022  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025
Cost-to-income  |  56.57%  |  55.02%  |  56.58%  |  58.70%
Loan-to-deposit  |  84.85%  |  81.98%  |  81.91%  |  78.94%
Credit loss ratio  |  0.84%  |  1.08%  |  0.83%  |  0.64%
e.g. 2025: 43,395 / 73,924 = 58.70%; 1,030,577 / 1,305,596 = 78.94%; 6,550 / 1,030,577 = 0.64%. [1.5]

Cost-to-income: above the 50% benchmark in every year and worsening from 55.02% (2023) to 58.70% (2025): operating expenses grew about 6.9% in 2025 against operating income growth of about 3.1%. Cost control is an efficiency weakness. [1]

Loan-to-deposit: falling from 84.85% to 78.94%, now below the 80% to 90% range. The bank is lending less of each rand of deposits and putting more into government bonds and other investments, i.e. moving away from its core business (weak loan demand at high rates, or a deliberate lower-risk allocation). This is also why asset utilisation and NIM are weak. Above 100% would instead mean lending more than deposits, funded by borrowing. [1]

Credit loss ratio: 1.08% in 2023 down to 0.64% in 2025, at or below the bottom of the 1% to 3% range, so credit risk is low and improving: this is a strength. [1]

parts.required: The template defines CET1 capital as share capital + capital reserve + retained income, and the CET1 ratio is provided. Calculate CET1 capital and the implied risk-weighted assets (RWA) for 2022 to 2025, and express RWA as a percentage of earning assets. What do the figures say about the bank's capital position?
parts.memo:
RWA = CET1 capital / CET1 ratio. [1]

  |  2022  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025
CET1 capital (Rm)  |  104,976  |  107,749  |  112,264  |  114,023
CET1 ratio (provided)  |  13.95%  |  13.47%  |  13.30%  |  12.90%
Implied RWA (Rm)  |  752,516  |  799,918  |  844,090  |  883,899
RWA as % of earning assets  |  63.05%  |  64.32%  |  62.79%  |  59.81%
e.g. 2025: CET1 = 12,392 + 7,045 + 94,586 = 114,023; RWA = 114,023 / 12.9% = 883,899; RWA / earning assets = 59.81%. Average RWA/earning assets = 62.49%. [2]

The CET1 ratio is well above the regulatory minimum (4.5% CET1 in the template; South African banks hold roughly 13%, a large buffer built up since 2008). It has however drifted down from 13.95% to 12.90%, consistent with rising leverage. The bank has capital to spare, which supports dividends, but excess capital also depresses ROE (the trade-off between safety and return). [1]

parts.required: Bank growth is linked to loan growth and market growth. Calculate the historical growth in loans for 2023 to 2025 and the relationship between loan growth and GDP growth. Using the GDP forecasts (2026F 5.3%, 2027F 4.4%, 2028F 5.0%, 2029F 5.4%), what loan growth does this relationship imply, and how does it compare with the growth rates chosen in the template (7.0%, 6.5%, 6.0%, 5.0%)?
parts.memo:
Loan growth = loans(t) / loans(t-1) - 1; relationship = loan growth / GDP growth (GDP entered as a percentage number, so the figures below are decimal loan growth per percentage point of GDP). [1]

  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025
Loan growth  |  1.07%  |  7.91%  |  7.11%
SA nominal GDP growth (%)  |  6.6  |  4.9  |  4.6
Loan growth / GDP growth  |  0.16  |  1.62  |  1.55
e.g. 2025: 1,030,577 / 962,184 - 1 = 7.11%; 0.0711 / 4.6 = 0.0155. Average of the three years = 0.0111. [1]

Implied growth = GDP forecast x average ratio: 2026F 5.87%, 2027F 4.87%, 2028F 5.54%, 2029F 5.98%. [1]

The template instead uses 7.0%, 6.5%, 6.0% and 5.0%, i.e. judgemental rates that start close to the recent loan growth (7.1% in 2025) and taper towards GDP growth. These are higher than the GDP-implied growth for 2026 to 2028; the low 2023 ratio (0.0016) pulls the average down and could be treated as an outlier. Whatever rates are chosen must be justified (SARB/MPC expectations, competition from digital banks) and kept reasonable. [1]

parts.required: Calculate total interest-earning assets (TIEA) and total interest-bearing liabilities (TIBL) for 2022 to 2025, the interest rate earned on assets and paid on liabilities each year, and the four-year average rates that will drive the forecast. (TIBL = due to banks + deposits + bonds issued + derivative financial liabilities.)
parts.memo:
TIEA is the same set of assets as the earning assets in Question 1 (cash + investments + loans); TIBL is the liabilities the bank pays interest on. Rate earned = interest income / TIEA; rate paid = interest expense / TIBL. [1]

  |  2022  |  2023  |  2024  |  2025  |  Average
TIEA (Rm)  |  1,193,531  |  1,243,657  |  1,344,283  |  1,477,724  |  
TIBL (Rm)  |  1,101,263  |  1,149,563  |  1,236,095  |  1,368,456  |  
Interest rate on IEA  |  6.88%  |  9.40%  |  9.30%  |  8.43%  |  8.50%
Interest rate on IBL  |  4.16%  |  6.56%  |  6.73%  |  5.97%  |  5.86%
e.g. 2025: 124,622 / 1,477,724 = 8.43%; 81,744 / 1,368,456 = 5.97%. [2]

Average rate earned = 8.50%; average rate paid = 5.86%. The forecast assumes these averages persist; the spread between them is squeezed by market interest rates and competition. [1]

parts.required: Forecast 2026F retained income using the average payout ratio (2022-2025) and net income from 2.4. Then check whether the forecast balance sheet balances. Explain how the template deals with any difference and which balancing figure is used.
parts.memo:
Payout ratio = dividends / net income: 57.09%, 57.13%, 57.07%, 57.49%; average 57.20%. [1]

2026F dividends = 57.20% x 18,210 = 10,416. Retained income = 94,586 + 18,210 - 10,416 = 102,381. Other equity lines are unchanged (no forecast of share issues or buy-backs), so total equity = 134,762. [1]

Balance check: total assets (with government bonds unchanged) = 1,645,306; total equity + liabilities before any plug = 1,622,193. Funding is short by 23,113. [1]

Equity and the loan/deposit forecasts are not changed, so the shortfall is plugged on the liability side: due to banks and other financial institutions increases by 23,113 (the bank would have to borrow; issuing more bonds would be an equally reasonable plug). If funding exceeded assets, the surplus would instead be invested in government bonds (the asset-side balancing figure). Both lines must be set to your own balancing items when the template is adapted. [1]

parts.required: The valuation only pays out dividends the bank can afford without breaching the minimum CET1 requirement. Using RWA = average RWA/TIEA (from Question 1.6) x forecast TIEA, minimum CET1 of 4.5% of RWA, and the net income and dividend forecasts for 2026F to 2029F (net income 18,210; 19,318; 20,498; 21,612), determine the dividend that can actually be paid each year.
parts.memo:
Forecast dividends = payout ratio x net income; CET1 capital = share capital + capital reserve + forecast retained income; RWA = average RWA/TIEA x TIEA; excess = CET1 - 4.5% x RWA; actual dividend = the lower of the excess capital and the forecast dividend. [2]

parts.required: Value the bank's equity using a dividend discount model: discount the dividends from 3.1 at the cost of equity from 1.4, with a terminal value for 2029F onward using a perpetual growth rate equal to the 2029F loan growth rate (5%). Calculate the equity value (Rm) and the intrinsic value per share.
parts.memo:
Cost of equity = 14.23%; terminal growth g = 5.0%. [1]

  |  2026F  |  2027F  |  2028F  |  2029F (terminal)
Dividend (Rm)  |  10,416  |  11,050  |  11,724  |  12,361
Discount factor  |  1/(1+14.23%)^1  |  1/(1+14.23%)^2  |  1/(1+14.23%)^3  |  1/(1+14.23%)^3
Present value (Rm)  |  9,118  |  8,468  |  7,865  |  89,828
PV of the 2026F to 2028F dividends = 9,118 + 8,468 + 7,865 = 25,451. [3]

The 2029F cash flow is treated as the first dividend of a growing perpetuity: terminal value = D(2029F) / (ke - g) = 12,361 / (14.232% - 5.0%) = 133,898, discounted with the three-year factor (1.1423^3) to give 89,828. This is much bigger than the other values because it contains all dividends from 2029F onward. [3]

Equity value = 25,451 + 89,828 = R115,279 million. [0.5]

Value per share = 115,279 x 1,000,000 / 456,904,901 = R252.30. [0.5]

parts.required: Compare the intrinsic value per share with the actual share price (R266.26) and the book value per share. What does the price-to-book ratio imply about value creation? What is the difference between price and book value, and what does the Bloomberg P/B of 1.1 imply for the share price?
parts.memo:
Book value per share = total equity / shares = 126,967 x 1,000,000 / 456,904,901 = R277.88. [1]

DDM value R252.30 is below the actual price of R266.26 (the shares trade about 5.5% above the DDM value, so on this model they look slightly overvalued) and below book value (DDM value / book = 0.91, actual price / book = 0.96). A P/B below 1 means the market believes the bank is destroying value; this is consistent with ROE (13.55%) being below the cost of equity (14.23%) from 1.4. If P/B = 1 the bank is just maintaining value and if above 1 it is creating value. [1.5]

Price is what investors are willing to pay (driven by expectations and beliefs); book value is what the equity is worth on the balance sheet. Banks mark their assets to market, so book value per share is in theory what each share would receive if the assets were sold and liabilities paid. Where price is below book value, options are to improve operations so ROE exceeds the cost of equity or, in the extreme, to liquidate and return the assets to shareholders. [0.5]

With Bloomberg's P/B of 1.1: implied share price = 1.1 x R277.88 = R305.67, which is above both the DDM value and the actual price, so the market data and the model are not consistent. Differences are normally explained by the forecast assumptions (growth, payout, cost of equity) and by the market expecting an improvement in returns. [1]

parts.required: Forecasts in the template are based on historical averages. When should you adjust these historical averages, and what care must you take when doing so?
parts.memo:
Historical averages assume that nothing significant changes in future. They should be adjusted where there is a reason to expect a different outcome, for example the CEO and CFO reports, the SARB/MPC outlook for inflation and interest rates, the competitive effect of digital banks, or a structural change in the market. [1]

Outliers: if one year is very different from the rest, something unusual happened in that year and it should be ignored so that it does not skew the average. Structural shifts: if the last two years are similar to each other but different from the earlier ones, argue that a fundamental shift occurred and base the forecast on the most recent years (this is why some ratios in the template use the average of the last two or three years only). Volatile banks need more judgement. [1]

Any change must be reasonable, explained and linked to a clear reason (e.g. an increase from 1.1% to 1.3% because the SARB is expected to raise rates); the exact size matters less than showing that you understand the driver. Do not use implausible numbers to engineer a result. [1]
